title: App Lifecycle, Background Work & Push Notifications
scopeHtml: Scope: App states, scenePhase, background modes, BGTaskScheduler, push (APNs), silent push, local notifications, WorkManager comparison.

notes.title: Baseline and the big mental shift
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Android you can run a foreground service with a notification, schedule WorkManager jobs, hold wake locks and receive FCM data messages, and the OS mostly lets a well-behaved app keep working (Doze and App Standby restrict it). In iOS there is no general-purpose background service. When the user leaves, the app is suspended within seconds and the system decides, by heuristics, when to give you short slices of time back.

Baseline. Swift 6, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum, SwiftUI-first with a UIKit AppDelegate where required (@UIApplicationDelegateAdaptor). Fast-moving or unconfirmed items (Live Activities, App Intents specifics, iOS 18/26 changes) are marked verify.

Android iOS
Foreground Service None general; narrow Background Modes (audio, location, VoIP...) or a Live Activity
WorkManager periodic/one-time BGAppRefreshTask, BGProcessingTask (BGTaskScheduler)
DownloadManager / WorkManager download Background URLSession
FCM (data + notification messages) APNs (alert push, silent push); FCM wraps APNs on iOS
NotificationChannel UNNotificationCategory + system per-app settings (no channels, but interruption levels)
Application.ActivityLifecycleCallbacks scenePhase, UIApplicationDelegate, UISceneDelegate
Process death + onSaveInstanceState Termination without callback + state restoration (@SceneStorage)

Real industry examples. Spotify and Apple Music use the audio background mode; Uber and Lyft use location mode plus Live Activities; WhatsApp and Signal rely on VoIP/notification service extensions; news apps depend on silent pushes and background refresh to prefetch content.

Everyday analogy. Android is a flat where you may leave a cooker on while out (with rules). iOS is a hotel: when you leave the room, housekeeping tidies up, and may pop in for a minute at times they choose.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "I will run a service to sync every 15 minutes". There is no such guarantee on iOS.
  • Treating BGTaskScheduler as exact alarms. It is an opportunistic hint.
  • Assuming the app is told when it is terminated.

notes.title: App states and the lifecycle
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Activity states onCreate/onStart/onResume/onPause/onStop/onDestroy and process death. iOS has app/scene states: Not running, Inactive, Active, Background, Suspended.

  Not running -> Inactive -> Active  <-> Inactive -> Background -> Suspended -> (killed silently)
                                                         |
                                  runs for a short time (~5 s grace, then up to ~30 s
                                  via beginBackgroundTask; verify) before suspension
  • Inactive: visible but not receiving events (incoming call, Control Center pulled down, app switcher).
  • Active: foreground and interactive.
  • Background: executing code but not visible (briefly after leaving, or when launched in the background by the system).
  • Suspended: in memory but frozen, zero CPU. The system may terminate suspended apps at any time to reclaim memory, WITHOUT calling any delegate method. Do not rely on applicationWillTerminate (called only in rare cases for non-suspended apps).

Since iOS 13 UI lifecycle is per scene (iPad multi-window), so you observe scene phases in SwiftUI:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@main
struct MyApp: App {
    @Environment(\.scenePhase) private var scenePhase
    @UIApplicationDelegateAdaptor(AppDelegate.self) var appDelegate

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup { ContentView() }
            .onChange(of: scenePhase) { _, phase in
                switch phase {
                case .active:     print("foreground, interactive")
                case .inactive:   print("visible but not interactive")
                case .background: print("save state now")   // flush DB, cancel timers
                @unknown default: break
                }
            }
    }
}
class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        ProcessLifecycleOwner.get().lifecycle.addObserver(LifecycleEventObserver { _, e ->
            when (e) {
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_START -> { /* foreground */ }
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_STOP -> { /* save state now */ }
                else -> {}
            }
        })
    }
}

scenePhase read at the App level reflects the aggregate of all scenes; read inside a View it reflects that scene. Legacy and still needed hooks live in UIApplicationDelegate: application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:) (SDK init: Firebase, Sentry), application(_:didRegisterForRemoteNotificationsWithDeviceToken:), application(_:handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession:completionHandler:), application(_:didReceiveRemoteNotification:fetchCompletionHandler:). SwiftUI has no equivalent for several of these, hence the delegate adaptor.

Launch types. Cold launch (process created), warm launch (process in memory). An app can also be launched into the background by the system (background fetch, silent push, location event, URLSession completion): your init and didFinishLaunching run with NO UI and scenePhase stays .background. Heavy startup work or UI assumptions there cause crashes visible only in Organizer, never in your foreground testing. Use UIApplication.shared.applicationState in the delegate if needed (main-actor isolated).

State restoration. Because the app can be terminated while suspended, users expect to return where they were. SwiftUI: @SceneStorage persists small per-scene values (selected tab, navigation path as Codable data, draft text) and restores them on relaunch, the counterpart of SavedStateHandle. For larger state, persist to disk in the .background transition. UIKit: stateRestorationActivity(for:) with NSUserActivity (the older encodeRestorableState APIs are deprecated, verify).

struct RootView: View {
    @SceneStorage("selectedTab") private var tab = 0
    @SceneStorage("draft") private var draft = ""
    var body: some View { /* TabView(selection: $tab) ... */ EmptyView() }
}

Real incidents.

  • Work lost on kill: state saved only in applicationWillTerminate, which never fires for suspended apps. Save at .background.
  • Double SDK initialization: a background launch plus a foreground launch initializing analytics twice; guard with a one-time flag.
  • Launch crash visible only from background launches: code touching UIApplication.shared.windows that do not exist.

Real industry examples. Google Maps and Apple Maps restore the previous camera position; Safari restores tabs; banking apps intentionally do NOT restore sensitive screens (they reset to login on .background, often overlaying a privacy view in the app switcher snapshot).

Everyday analogy. Leaving a library desk: you must leave a bookmark in your book before you step out; staff might clear the desk while you are away without telling you.

Common interview traps.

  • Relying on applicationWillTerminate.
  • Confusing inactive with background.
  • Mixing app delegate lifecycle (pre-iOS 13) with scene lifecycle.
  • Assuming code in init of App only runs for user launches.

notes.title: Staying alive briefly: background modes and finite-length tasks
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Foreground service started when the user leaves the app. iOS gives you (a) a short grace period plus a finite task assertion and (b) a short list of declared Background Modes for specific use-cases.

Finite-length task (about 30 seconds in practice, verify; never rely on more):

@MainActor
func flushAnalytics() {
    var taskID = UIBackgroundTaskIdentifier.invalid
    taskID = UIApplication.shared.beginBackgroundTask(withName: "flush") {
        // expiration handler: clean up, you are about to be suspended
        UIApplication.shared.endBackgroundTask(taskID)
        taskID = .invalid
    }
    Task {
        await uploader.flush()
        UIApplication.shared.endBackgroundTask(taskID)   // always end it, even on success
        taskID = .invalid
    }
}

In Swift 6 ProcessInfo.processInfo.performExpiringActivity(withReason:using:) is an alternative for short work, and Task can start inside beginBackgroundTask. Failing to call endBackgroundTask leads to a watchdog kill with termination reason "background task assertion timeout" (the app took too long to suspend); this shows as exception code 0x8badf00d ("ate bad food") in crash logs.

Background Modes (Signing & Capabilities > Background Modes, written to UIBackgroundModes in Info.plist):

<key>UIBackgroundModes</key>
<array>
    <string>audio</string>
    <string>location</string>
    <string>voip</string>
    <string>fetch</string>
    <string>processing</string>
    <string>remote-notification</string>
    <string>bluetooth-central</string>
</array>
Mode Use App Review rule
audio music, podcasts, navigation voice Must actually play audio
location turn-by-turn, run tracking Needs justification and the "Always" permission flow
voip calls (PushKit + CallKit) Must report incoming call to CallKit immediately, or the app is killed and PushKit pushes throttled (iOS 13+)
fetch / processing BGTaskScheduler (below) declare identifiers in BGTaskSchedulerPermittedIdentifiers
remote-notification silent pushes see silent pushes section
bluetooth-central/peripheral BLE devices needs actual use
external-accessory, nearby-interaction specific accessories

Misusing a mode (e.g. playing silent audio to keep the app alive) is a known App Store rejection reason (guideline 2.5.4) and may also be reviewed as battery abuse.

Real industry examples. Spotify (audio), Strava (location), WhatsApp and Skype (VoIP + CallKit), Garmin Connect (bluetooth).

Everyday analogy. Finite task: asking the shop for five more minutes to finish packing before closing. Background modes: shops that legally stay open for specific reasons (pharmacy, hospital).

Common interview traps.

  • Starting a background task and never ending it (0x8badf00d).
  • Declaring a mode without genuine use and failing review.
  • Assuming a foreground-service-like keep-alive exists.
  • VoIP push without reporting a CallKit call.

notes.title: BGTaskScheduler: refresh and processing tasks
notes.html:
Android equivalent. WorkManager periodic work with constraints (network, charging). BGTaskScheduler (iOS 13+) is similar but with far less control: you submit a request with an earliest begin date; the system decides when (and whether) to run based on app usage patterns, battery, charging, network, Low Power Mode.

Two types:

  • BGAppRefreshTaskRequest: short (about 30 s) fetch to keep content fresh. The system learns when the user opens the app (e.g. mornings) and schedules shortly before. Runs even if the app is not frequently used? No: apps the user rarely opens get few or no runs.
  • BGProcessingTaskRequest: minutes-long work (database maintenance, ML model training, large syncs) typically while charging and idle; flags requiresNetworkConnectivity and requiresExternalPower.

Setup:

  1. Add fetch and/or processing modes.
  2. Register identifiers in Info.plist BGTaskSchedulerPermittedIdentifiers.
  3. Register the handler BEFORE the app finishes launching (in didFinishLaunching, or the App init) and submit requests when going to background.
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import BackgroundTasks

enum BG {
    static let refreshID = "com.acme.app.refresh"

    static func register() {
        BGTaskScheduler.shared.register(forTaskWithIdentifier: refreshID, using: nil) { task in
            handleRefresh(task as! BGAppRefreshTask)
        }
    }

    static func schedule() {
        let request = BGAppRefreshTaskRequest(identifier: refreshID)
        request.earliestBeginDate = Date(timeIntervalSinceNow: 15 * 60)   // a hint, not a promise
        do { try BGTaskScheduler.shared.submit(request) }
        catch { print("BG submit failed: \(error)") }                     // e.g. notPermitted / tooManyPendingTaskRequests
    }

    static func handleRefresh(_ task: BGAppRefreshTask) {
        schedule()                                // reschedule first: the chain breaks otherwise
        let work = Task {
            do {
                try await Syncer.shared.refresh()
                task.setTaskCompleted(success: true)
            } catch {
                task.setTaskCompleted(success: false)
            }
        }
        task.expirationHandler = { work.cancel() }   // time is up: stop cooperatively
    }
}
val request = PeriodicWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>(15, TimeUnit.MINUTES)
    .setConstraints(Constraints.Builder().setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.CONNECTED).build())
    .build()
WorkManager.getInstance(ctx).enqueueUniquePeriodicWork("sync", ExistingPeriodicWorkPolicy.KEEP, request)

Call BG.schedule() from .onChange(of: scenePhase) when entering .background. SwiftUI also offers the .backgroundTask(.appRefresh("id")) { } scene modifier that runs an async closure (iOS 16+; verify cancellation behaviour) which removes the manual expirationHandler and setTaskCompleted.

Rules and limits.

  • earliestBeginDate is a minimum; the real run may be hours later or never. Do not use for time-critical events (use push).
  • Tasks are only run for apps that are NOT force-quit by the user (swiping the app away in the switcher cancels background refresh until the next launch).
  • Max pending requests per type is limited (about 1 refresh, 10 processing; verify). Duplicates throw tooManyPendingTaskRequests.
  • If the system never invokes your task, check Settings > General > Background App Refresh (user or Low Power Mode can disable it) and UIApplication.shared.backgroundRefreshStatus.
  • Data Protection: the device may be locked; files must use completeFileProtectionUntilFirstUserAuthentication and Keychain items AfterFirstUnlock or reads fail.

Debugging. You cannot wait 15 minutes. With the app running and paused in the debugger, run in the LLDB console:

e -l objc -- (void)[[BGTaskScheduler sharedScheduler] _simulateLaunchForTaskWithIdentifier:@"com.acme.app.refresh"]

and _simulateExpirationForTaskWithIdentifier: to test the expiration path (private selectors, debug only). Xcode's Instruments has no BG scheduler instrument; use os_log plus MetricKit's MXBackgroundExitData (cumulativeBackgroundTaskAssertionTimeoutExitCount and similar fields) from the Organizer to see kills.

Real industry examples. News and weather apps (NYT, Carrot Weather) prefetch content; Apple Photos uses processing tasks for indexing; Dropbox-style apps use processing while charging to run uploads. Spotify downloads use background URLSession instead because transfers are the OS's job.

Everyday analogy. You leave a note for the cleaner, "come in the afternoon if you can". They may come, may choose another day, and will not come at all if you told the concierge you never want visitors (force quit).

Common interview traps.

  • Believing earliestBeginDate is an exact schedule.
  • Not rescheduling inside the handler.
  • Registering the task after launch finished (crash: "all launch handlers must be registered before application finishes launching").
  • Forgetting setTaskCompleted, leading to future throttling.
  • Testing only in the simulator: BG tasks do not run there.

notes.title: Background URLSession and long transfers
notes.html:
Android equivalent. WorkManager + foreground service for uploads, or DownloadManager. In iOS the system daemon performs transfers for a .background(withIdentifier:) session even when your app is suspended or was terminated by the system. The full mechanism (delegate, handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession, discretionary flag, resume data) is covered in the networking notes (see also 01_N1); here is the lifecycle summary.

@main
struct MyApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup { ContentView() }
            .backgroundTask(.urlSession("com.acme.app.uploads")) {
                // runs when the system relaunches the app to deliver events (iOS 16+, verify)
                await TransferManager.shared.handleBackgroundEvents()
            }
    }
}

Lifecycle:

 enqueue task -> app suspended / terminated by system -> nsurlsessiond transfers
   -> finished: system relaunches app in background (about 30 s of runtime)
   -> app recreates session with the SAME identifier -> delegate callbacks
   -> call the saved completion handler when urlSessionDidFinishEvents fires

Remember: force-quit by the user cancels the transfers; isDiscretionary lets the system delay for Wi-Fi/charging; sessionSendsLaunchEvents lets the system launch you.

Choosing the right tool for background work.

Need Tool
Upload/download big file Background URLSession
Fetch small fresh content BGAppRefreshTask or silent push
Maintenance / ML while charging BGProcessingTask
Finish a short task after leaving beginBackgroundTask
Receive time-critical info Alert push (with service extension)
Track location Location background mode / Significant-change service
Play audio / call Audio / VoIP modes

Real industry examples. Google Photos and iCloud Photos upload backups; Spotify/Apple Podcasts download episodes; Nextcloud/Dropbox camera upload.

Everyday analogy. A freight company collects and delivers the crate while you are away, and rings your doorbell when it is done.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a default session for a 200 MB upload and losing it at suspension.
  • Creating the session twice with the same identifier.
  • Not calling the completion handler (system throttles future launches).

notes.title: APNs architecture, device tokens and FCM
notes.html:
Android equivalent. FCM: the app obtains a registration token, your server sends a message via FCM, Google Play services delivers it. On iOS the transport is APNs (Apple Push Notification service) and is the ONLY way to wake the device; FCM on iOS is a layer on top of APNs, not a replacement.

  App -> UIApplication.registerForRemoteNotifications()
      <- APNs device token (hex bytes) delivered to AppDelegate
  App -> sends token to YOUR backend
  Backend -> HTTP/2 POST to APNs (api.push.apple.com:443/3/device/<token>) with auth + payload
  APNs -> device -> system shows banner / wakes app (silent) / launches notification extension

Facts:

  • Registering. Add the Push Notifications capability (entitlement aps-environment: development or production). Request permission with UNUserNotificationCenter.current().requestAuthorization(options: [.alert, .badge, .sound]) (prompt shown once; if denied the user must go to Settings), then call registerForRemoteNotifications().
final class AppDelegate: NSObject, UIApplicationDelegate {
    func application(_ app: UIApplication,
                     didFinishLaunchingWithOptions opts: [UIApplication.LaunchOptionsKey: Any]? = nil) -> Bool {
        UNUserNotificationCenter.current().delegate = NotificationRouter.shared
        return true
    }
    func application(_ app: UIApplication,
                     didRegisterForRemoteNotificationsWithDeviceToken token: Data) {
        let hex = token.map { String(format: "%02x", $0) }.joined()
        Task { try? await API.registerPushToken(hex) }
    }
    func application(_ app: UIApplication,
                     didFailToRegisterForRemoteNotificationsWithError error: Error) {
        // simulator without APNs, missing entitlement, no network
    }
}

@MainActor
func askForPush() async {
    let granted = (try? await UNUserNotificationCenter.current()
        .requestAuthorization(options: [.alert, .badge, .sound])) ?? false
    if granted { UIApplication.shared.registerForRemoteNotifications() }
}
  • Device token. Opaque, up to roughly 100 bytes; it can change (restore from backup, reinstall, OS update), so send it to your server on every launch and let the server dedupe. Do not assume 32 bytes. Tokens differ between sandbox (development builds) and production (TestFlight/App Store): sending a production token to the sandbox host returns BadDeviceToken, the top cause of "push works in Xcode, not in TestFlight".
  • Provider auth. Token-based (.p8 key, JWT signed ES256, valid up to 60 minutes, one key works for all your apps and both environments) preferred over certificate-based (.p12, expires yearly, per app). FCM asks you to upload the APNs key.
  • Required headers: apns-topic (bundle id; for Live Activity push .push-type.liveactivity, for VoIP .voip), apns-push-type (alert, background, voip, liveactivity...), apns-priority (10 immediate, 5 power-considerate; background pushes MUST use 5), apns-expiration, apns-collapse-id.
  • Payload limit: 4 KB (VoIP 5 KB).
{
  "aps": {
    "alert": { "title": "Order shipped", "body": "Arriving Friday" },
    "badge": 3,
    "sound": "default",
    "category": "ORDER",
    "thread-id": "order-1234",
    "mutable-content": 1,
    "interruption-level": "time-sensitive"
  },
  "orderId": "1234"
}

FCM on iOS. Add the Firebase SDK, upload the APNs key in the console, and the SDK swizzles (or you forward) the APNs token mapping it to an FCM registration token. If method swizzling is disabled (FirebaseAppDelegateProxyEnabled = NO) you must pass the token manually: Messaging.messaging().apnsToken = deviceToken. A common bug is data messages (no notification block) not arriving in the background: on iOS FCM data-only messages are delivered as silent pushes (content-available), subject to throttling. Third parties (OneSignal, Braze, Airship) also route through APNs.

Real industry examples. Instagram, Slack and Uber run their own APNs providers over HTTP/2 with connection pooling; smaller apps use FCM or OneSignal. WhatsApp and Signal send only a content-free "wake" push and the notification extension fetches the encrypted message.

Everyday analogy. APNs is the postal sorting office of one nationwide mail service (Apple's). The device token is your house's mailbox number, which can be reassigned, so you tell the sender the current number every time.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing sandbox and production tokens/hosts.
  • Believing FCM replaces APNs on iOS.
  • Hardcoding a 32-byte token length.
  • Sending background pushes with priority 10 (APNs rejects or throttles).
  • Expecting the permission prompt to reappear after denial.

notes.title: Local and remote notifications: UNUserNotificationCenter, actions, service extensions
notes.html:
Android equivalent. NotificationCompat.Builder, channels, PendingIntents and action buttons, RemoteInput for inline reply. iOS centralises everything in UNUserNotificationCenter.

Local notification:

func scheduleReminder() async throws {
    let content = UNMutableNotificationContent()
    content.title = "Stand up"
    content.body = "You have been sitting for an hour"
    content.sound = .default
    content.categoryIdentifier = "REMINDER"
    content.threadIdentifier = "health"

    let trigger = UNTimeIntervalNotificationTrigger(timeInterval: 3600, repeats: false)
    // also UNCalendarNotificationTrigger, UNLocationNotificationTrigger
    let request = UNNotificationRequest(identifier: UUID().uuidString, content: content, trigger: trigger)
    try await UNUserNotificationCenter.current().add(request)
}

Local notifications are scheduled with the OS (limit of 64 pending per app; the system keeps the soonest, verify), so they fire even if the app is terminated, which makes them the reliable way to remind a user at a time, unlike BGTaskScheduler.

Foreground presentation and tap handling (delegate set in didFinishLaunching, always before the app finishes launching, otherwise taps that launch the app are missed):

@MainActor
final class NotificationRouter: NSObject, UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate {
    static let shared = NotificationRouter()

    // App is in foreground: choose whether to show it
    nonisolated func userNotificationCenter(_ center: UNUserNotificationCenter,
        willPresent notification: UNNotification) async -> UNNotificationPresentationOptions {
        [.banner, .sound, .list]    // iOS 14+ names; nothing returned = silent in foreground
    }

    // User tapped the notification or pressed an action
    nonisolated func userNotificationCenter(_ center: UNUserNotificationCenter,
        didReceive response: UNNotificationResponse) async {
        let info = response.notification.request.content.userInfo
        switch response.actionIdentifier {
        case "REPLY":
            if let reply = response as? UNTextInputNotificationResponse {
                await send(reply.userText, info)
            }
        case UNNotificationDefaultActionIdentifier:
            await Router.shared.open(deepLink: info["link"] as? String)
        default: break
        }
    }
}

Categories and actions (registered once at launch):

let reply = UNTextInputNotificationAction(identifier: "REPLY", title: "Reply",
                                          options: [], textInputButtonTitle: "Send", textInputPlaceholder: "Message")
let mute = UNNotificationAction(identifier: "MUTE", title: "Mute", options: [.destructive])
let category = UNNotificationCategory(identifier: "MESSAGE", actions: [reply, mute],
                                      intentIdentifiers: [], options: [])
UNUserNotificationCenter.current().setNotificationCategories([category])

Interruption levels (iOS 15+): passive, active, timeSensitive (needs entitlement com.apple.developer.usernotifications.time-sensitive), critical (needs special Apple approval entitlement). These replace Android's channel importance. Users control per-app settings: Immediate Delivery, Scheduled Summary, Focus filters; you cannot force them.

Service extension (UNNotificationServiceExtension). A separate app extension target that receives a push with "mutable-content": 1 before display, with roughly 30 seconds, to modify the content: download and attach an image, decrypt an end-to-end encrypted body, increment local state.

final class NotificationService: UNNotificationServiceExtension {
    var contentHandler: ((UNNotificationContent) -> Void)?
    var best: UNMutableNotificationContent?

    override func didReceive(_ request: UNNotificationRequest,
                             withContentHandler handler: @escaping (UNNotificationContent) -> Void) {
        contentHandler = handler
        best = request.content.mutableCopy() as? UNMutableNotificationContent
        guard let best, let urlStr = request.content.userInfo["image"] as? String,
              let url = URL(string: urlStr) else { return handler(request.content) }
        Task {
            if let (tmp, _) = try? await URLSession.shared.download(from: url),
               let att = try? UNNotificationAttachment(identifier: "img", url: tmp) {
                best.attachments = [att]
            }
            handler(best)
        }
    }
    override func serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire() {
        if let handler = contentHandler, let best { handler(best) }   // deliver what you have
    }
}

Limits: about 24 MB memory for the extension (exceeding gets it killed and the unmodified push shown, verify); shares data with the app only via App Group and Keychain access group; the extension can NOT run on silent pushes (it needs an alert). A notification content extension (UNNotificationContentExtension) renders a custom UI when the user long-presses. Rich notifications and Communication Notifications (INSendMessageIntent donation) add avatars and Focus handling.

Badge counts are set by the payload's badge field or UNUserNotificationCenter.current().setBadgeCount(_:) (iOS 16+); the server usually tracks unread count, otherwise the extension updates a shared counter.

Real industry examples. WhatsApp, Signal and Slack decrypt in the service extension; Instagram attaches images; Uber and DoorDash use time-sensitive for ride and delivery arrivals; Duolingo schedules local notifications for streak reminders.

Everyday analogy. The service extension is a receptionist who opens each parcel, adds a nameplate or photo and hands it on within a time limit; if she runs out of time she hands over what she has.

Common interview traps.

  • Setting the notification delegate too late, losing the tap that cold-launched the app.
  • Expecting the service extension to run for silent pushes or without mutable-content.
  • Exceeding extension memory or time and silently getting the plain notification.
  • Trying to create channels: they do not exist; use categories and interruption levels.

notes.title: Silent pushes and why delivery is not guaranteed
notes.html:
Android equivalent. FCM high-priority data messages can wake the app to run work (subject to Doze and App Standby buckets). On iOS, a silent push ("content-available": 1, no alert/sound/badge, apns-push-type: background, apns-priority: 5) lets the system launch/wake your app for about 30 seconds to fetch content.

{ "aps": { "content-available": 1 }, "syncToken": "abc" }
func application(_ app: UIApplication,
                 didReceiveRemoteNotification userInfo: [AnyHashable: Any]) async -> UIBackgroundFetchResult {
    do {
        let changed = try await Syncer.shared.pull(token: userInfo["syncToken"] as? String)
        return changed ? .newData : .noData
    } catch { return .failed }
}

Requirements: Remote notifications background mode, capability on, and not force-quit by the user.

Why delivery is not guaranteed.

  • APNs stores only the latest silent push per device when offline and may drop or coalesce older ones (collapse-id, the stored-notification rules), and throttles low-priority pushes.
  • The system budgets silent pushes per app (documented as a few per hour; real number depends on device state and app usage, verify; Apple says "do not send more than two or three per hour").
  • Low Power Mode, Background App Refresh disabled, the thermal state, and a user swiping the app away all block delivery to your code.
  • If your handler is slow or the app consumes too much power, the system learns and throttles.
  • No ordering or delivery confirmation exists.

Design implications: treat silent push as a hint to sync, never as the data channel. Make the sync idempotent and pull-based (cursor/ETag), and ALSO sync on foreground, on BGAppRefreshTask, and on the visible-alert path. For truly important messages use an alert push (optionally with mutable-content, so the service extension can fetch details), which APNs delivers reliably with high priority.

Testing. Use real device builds (the simulator supports .apns payload drag-and-drop in Xcode 11.4+, verify, but not APNs delivery) and tools such as Push Notifications Tester apps or xcrun simctl push <device> <bundleId> payload.json. Compare "silent works in debug with Xcode attached, but not on release": debugging disables throttling.

Real industry examples. Chat apps use alert pushes with extensions rather than silent-only; email clients (Spark, Gmail) use silent pushes to fetch and then post a local notification, and accept occasional delays; Apple's own documentation explicitly warns that silent notifications are not for continuous delivery.

Everyday analogy. A silent push is a tap on the shoulder from a neighbour: if you are asleep (throttled) or he tapped too often, you may not wake.

Common interview traps.

  • Using silent push for chat message delivery.
  • Sending priority 10 with content-available only.
  • Testing only with Xcode attached.
  • Claiming a push "guarantees" the app runs.

notes.title: Live Activities, App Intents and watchdog kills (verify)
notes.html:
Live Activities (iOS 16.1+; verify details). Real-time information on the Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island (iPhone 14 Pro+), built with ActivityKit and a widget extension using SwiftUI. Android analogue: ongoing notification or a foreground-service notification with live updates.

import ActivityKit

struct DeliveryAttributes: ActivityAttributes {
    struct ContentState: Codable, Hashable { var status: String; var etaMinutes: Int }
    var orderID: String
}

func startLiveActivity() throws {
    let attrs = DeliveryAttributes(orderID: "1234")
    let state = DeliveryAttributes.ContentState(status: "Preparing", etaMinutes: 25)
    let activity = try Activity.request(
        attributes: attrs,
        content: .init(state: state, staleDate: nil),
        pushType: .token)                       // request a push token to update remotely
    Task {
        for await tokenData in activity.pushTokenUpdates {
            let token = tokenData.map { String(format: "%02x", $0) }.joined()
            try? await API.registerLiveActivity(token, orderID: "1234")
        }
    }
}

Updates come from the app (activity.update(...)) while it runs, or from your server via APNs with apns-push-type: liveactivity, topic <bundleId>.push-type.liveactivity, and payload {"aps":{"timestamp":..., "event":"update", "content-state":{...}}}. Rules: up to 8 hours active (plus up to 4 hours on the Lock Screen after ending; verify), a 4 KB state size limit, update budgets (high-priority pushes are rate-limited; add NSSupportsLiveActivitiesFrequentUpdates for more, verify), user can disable per app. Used by Uber, DoorDash, sports score apps, Apple Maps. Push-to-start tokens and iOS 18/26 changes are fast-moving: verify.

App Intents (iOS 16+). The modern framework for exposing actions to Shortcuts, Siri, Spotlight, widgets and the Action button. Android analogue: App Actions / shortcuts.

import AppIntents

struct AddTaskIntent: AppIntent {
    static let title: LocalizedStringResource = "Add Task"
    @Parameter(title: "Title") var title: String

    func perform() async throws -> some IntentResult {
        try await TaskStore.shared.add(title)
        return .result()
    }
}

Intents run in your app's process (or an extension), may be launched in the background without UI, so apply the same background-launch caution. AppShortcutsProvider registers phrases for Siri without user setup. Interactive widgets and Live Activity buttons (iOS 17+) run AppIntents. Anything on Siri/Apple Intelligence integration is evolving: verify.

Watchdog and termination reasons. The system kills (no callback) apps for:

Signature Meaning Fix
0x8badf00d Watchdog: launch, resume or a background task took too long (launch about 20 s, background transitions seconds) Move heavy work off main thread; end background tasks
0xdead10cc App held a file lock/SQLite handle in a shared container while suspended Release locks on .background, avoid WAL in app group on suspend, use beginBackgroundTask for DB close
0xc00010ff Thermal kill Lower CPU/GPU usage
Jetsam (memory) Exceeded memory limit; no crash report, shows in Organizer/MetricKit as memory termination Reduce footprint, respond to memory warnings (UIApplication.didReceiveMemoryWarningNotification), Instruments Allocations/VM Tracker
0xbaadca11 PushKit VoIP push not reported to CallKit Report the call immediately
0xbad22222 VoIP app resumed too frequently (older) Reduce wakeups

Background execution limits to remember: about 30 s for finite tasks and BG refresh, minutes for processing (and the system can cancel at any time via expirationHandler), a handful of seconds to respond to a notification-extension, and strict memory ceilings (extensions and widgets have much lower limits, typically tens of MB; verify numbers). MetricKit (MXMetricManager, MXDiagnosticPayload, MXBackgroundExitData) and the Xcode Organizer (Crashes, Energy, Terminations) report these in production; Sentry/Crashlytics record watchdog events with their own detectors.

Real industry examples. Uber and DoorDash migrate order-tracking from polling to Live Activity pushes; Facebook published its work on out-of-memory (OOM) detection for iOS; Signal tuned notification extension memory to avoid being killed mid-decrypt.

Everyday analogy. The watchdog is a lifeguard with a whistle: if you take too long to respond (blocking the main thread at launch) or hold the pool lock when the pool closes (file lock while suspended), you are pulled out with no warning.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating Live Activities as a way to keep the app running; it only shows content, updated by app time or push.
  • Mixing up 0x8badf00d (time) and 0xdead10cc (locks).
  • Assuming memory kills produce stack traces.
  • Running heavy work in App Intents invoked from Siri/Shortcuts without testing background launch.

notes.title: Production patterns and interview checklist
notes.html:
Recommended architecture for "keep data fresh".

 1. Foreground: sync on .active scenePhase (cheap, ETag/cursor)
 2. Alert push (+ mutable-content service extension) for important events
 3. Silent push as a hint to sync early, never required
 4. BGAppRefreshTask as a daily-ish safety net
 5. BGProcessingTask for heavy maintenance (charging)
 6. Background URLSession for big files
 7. Local notifications for time-based reminders

This mirrors Android advice (FCM + WorkManager), but you must lower expectations of timing and prepare for "never runs".

Android to iOS translation answers.

  • "How would you sync every 15 minutes?" There is no guarantee; use foreground sync, push hints, and BGAppRefresh as best effort; if the product truly needs frequent updates use location or push-driven design.
  • "How do you keep a download going?" Background URLSession.
  • "How do you play music in background?" Audio mode plus AVAudioSession category .playback.
  • "How do you run code when the user kills the app?" You can't; saved state must already be persisted; significant location change and push can relaunch you only if the user did not force-quit.

Checklist before release.

  • Capabilities: Push, Background Modes (only used ones), App Groups, entitlements match provisioning profile and aps-environment production in release.
  • Permissions: purpose strings for location, Face ID; notification prompt timed after value is shown (pre-permission screen increases opt-in).
  • Token handling: sandbox vs production host, upload tokens each launch, remove token on logout.
  • Delegate set before launch ends; categories registered; deep link router handles cold launch from notification.
  • Background-launch safe init; data protection class and Keychain accessibility suitable for locked-device access.
  • Telemetry: MetricKit subscriber, Organizer terminations, push delivery analytics via apns-id and server logs.
  • Test matrix: foreground, background, suspended, terminated by system, force-quit, locked, Low Power Mode, airplane mode.

Typical incidents.

  • "Pushes stopped for some users": APNs returned Unregistered (410) after uninstall; server must prune the token on 410 and BadDeviceToken.
  • "Notification tap does nothing on cold start": delegate assigned in a view's onAppear, after the response was delivered.
  • "Duplicate notifications": both FCM and a local notification path posting.
  • "Push works for me, not for customers": production certificate/key mismatch, topic mismatch, or the app built with a development provisioning profile.
  • "Battery drain complaints": silent pushes with heavy work; background location left on; polling timers kept alive via audio tricks.

Real industry examples. Airbnb, Uber and Slack engineering blogs describe token hygiene, push-delivery observability and server-side retries as the main work, more than client code. Apple's own Human Interface Guidelines advise sparing, valuable notifications; over-notifying reduces opt-in.

Everyday analogy. Think of it as running a restaurant with an unpredictable delivery van: you cannot demand when it arrives, so you keep a pantry (local data), place orders in advance (push hints), and still check the door yourself when you open (foreground sync).

Common interview traps.

  • Designing as if the app is always running.
  • Forgetting to prune dead tokens.
  • No telemetry for terminations.
  • Answering with Android constructs (Service, WakeLock, AlarmManager exact) without the iOS limits.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• iOS suspends apps seconds after they leave the foreground and may terminate them silently; there is no foreground-service equivalent, only finite tasks, a short list of Background Modes and system-scheduled tasks.
  • Observe scenePhase (.active, .inactive, .background), save state when entering .background, never rely on applicationWillTerminate, and persist small UI state with @SceneStorage.
  • BGAppRefreshTask (about 30 s) and BGProcessingTask (minutes, charging) are opportunistic: register before launch finishes, add identifiers to Info.plist, reschedule inside the handler, handle expirationHandler, and test with the LLDB simulate commands.
  • Big transfers go through a background URLSession (delegate-only, stable identifier, completion handler, cancelled by force quit).
  • APNs is the only wake-up transport; FCM wraps it. Handle device tokens carefully (change over time, sandbox vs production, prune on 410), use p8 token auth, respect the 4 KB payload and header rules.
  • UNUserNotificationCenter handles local and remote notifications: set the delegate early, use categories for actions, interruption levels instead of channels, and a UNNotificationServiceExtension with mutable-content for images and decryption within its time and memory limits.
  • Silent pushes are throttled hints, not guaranteed delivery: make sync idempotent and pull-based, and back it up with foreground sync and BG tasks.
  • Live Activities (ActivityKit, APNs liveactivity) and App Intents extend your presence without background execution; their specifics change often, so verify per iOS version.
  • Know the watchdog and termination signatures (0x8badf00d, 0xdead10cc, jetsam, 0xbaadca11) and use Organizer and MetricKit to find them.
  • Verify before relying on: exact time budgets (about 30 s), pending-task limits, silent push rate guidance, Live Activity duration and update limits, SwiftUI .backgroundTask behaviour, simulator push support.
